name: FYP FX
tagline: Effects, captions and templates for vertical short-form video aimed at TikTok and Reels creators.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The mechanical core of a short-form effects tool is ffmpeg plus a speech-to-text model, and both are free and local. An agent can give you burned-in animated captions, zoom punches, speed ramps, shake, and a 9:16 export pipeline in a weekend, and that covers most of what people actually use. What it will not give you is a curated library of trend-matched presets that look like what is working on the feed this month, which is the part creators are really renting. You also lose phone-native editing, which matters when the whole workflow happens on a phone. Verdict stands as kinda mostly because the taste layer is the product and taste does not come out of a one-shot prompt.
coreLoopDIY: Drop in a vertical video, get auto-transcribed animated captions plus a handful of preset motion and audio effects, rendered out as an MP4.
requirements: Python 3.11 and a few GB of disk for the speech model
A machine that can transcode video without you walking away for an hour
Fonts you actually have the right to burn into video
whatYouLose: A preset library tuned to whatever is trending right now, updated by people who watch the feed for a living
Mobile editing, which is where most short-form editing actually happens
Fast cloud rendering; local exports of long clips will test your patience
Licensed fonts, sounds and template packs that come with the paid product
Someone else's opinion about what looks good, which is worth more than most people admit
moatNotes: Effect tools live or die on preset taste and on having clearance for the fonts and sounds baked into the templates.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part was never the video pipeline. Anyone can stack ffmpeg filters, but knowing which caption style, zoom cadence and sound cue reads as native on the feed this quarter is a full-time observation job, and the subscription is how you outsource it. Add the fact that creators edit on their phones between other work, and a local Python renderer stops being a replacement and starts being a hobby.
notes: The renderer is a weekend; the preset taste is a subscription to someone else's attention span.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user short-form video effects tool. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Python 3.11, FastAPI backend, plain HTML + vanilla JS frontend served by FastAPI.
- ffmpeg and ffprobe via subprocess for all video work. Do not use moviepy.
- faster-whisper (small.en by default) for transcription, model path configurable in .env.
- SQLite via sqlite3 stdlib for a simple job table. No ORM.

Functionality, in scope:
1. Upload a video file through the web UI. Store it under ./media/input.
2. Probe it with ffprobe, show duration, resolution and fps.
3. Transcribe audio with faster-whisper at word level timestamps. Cache the JSON next to the file so re-renders skip transcription.
4. Render burned-in animated captions: word-by-word pop-in, 2 to 4 words visible at a time, centered lower third, thick outline, configurable font file and color. Implement with ffmpeg drawtext filters generated from the word timestamps. Escape text properly.
5. Three effect presets applied on top, selectable per render: punch-zoom on caption boundaries, speed ramp (1.0x body, 1.5x on a user-marked range), and a subtle handheld shake. Each should be a documented ffmpeg filter chain in a single effects.py file.
6. Export 1080x1920 H.264 MP4, letterbox or center-crop the source, choice exposed in the UI.
7. Render runs as a background task, job status polls from the UI, finished files land in ./media/output with a download link.

Out of scope, do not build: mobile app, timeline scrubbing UI, multi-track editing, stock music, auto-posting to any platform, user auth.

Config in .env: MODEL_SIZE, FONT_PATH, OUTPUT_DIR. Ship a .env.example and a README with the exact ffmpeg version assumptions and one `python -m venv` quickstart. Include two sample renders in the README description so I can tell if it worked.
